concept: Search Node network transfer and multi-region cost
summary: Source-anchored research for Search Node network transfer and multi-region cost. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: MongoDB's 2024 engineering guidance uses regional and availability-zone replica-set tags with secondary read preferences to improve locality, with fallback when preferred nodes are unavailable. This is conditional secondary-read guidance, not proof that all search or write traffic becomes local. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-08-30)

Atlas recommends placing applications in the same provider and region, using nearest read preference when cross-region reads are necessary, limiting returned fields, and enabling client network compression. Atlas also states that intra-cluster communication is always compressed. These are optimizations, not evidence that all search traffic becomes free. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

MongoDB's multi-region Search Node announcement (August 14, 2024, updated March 6, 2025) describes Search Nodes as dedicated infrastructure for Atlas Search and Vector Search that scale search and database needs independently, and says multi-region availability provides redundancy against outages. A consolidation comparison should price equivalent geographic availability on both sides rather than comparing one region against several (this is a modeling inference). Sources: https://mongodb.com/blog/post/atlas-search-nodes-now-with-multi-region-availability

For a TCO comparison, measure the actual transfer volume between Search Nodes and database nodes and apply the relevant per-GB rate separately from Search Node capacity; Atlas data transfer pricing varies by cloud provider and by the region of the source and destination nodes. This is an inference; the sources provide no universal network-savings percentage for Atlas versus a separate search/vector service. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/search-node.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs.md

Atlas bills network traffic between dedicated Search Nodes and database nodes. These charges appear in cluster-level data transfer, without a separate Search Node transfer breakdown; consolidation therefore does not imply zero internal search-network cost. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Atlas transfer charges depend on provider and source/destination regions, and multi-region clusters can incur higher transfer costs. Model application traffic and internal Search Node traffic separately before aggregating the cluster bill. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/search-node.md

Atlas requires at least two Search Nodes per region and supports counts per region per shard. Its multi-region configuration uses the same search tier across regions and deploys the specified count in each region containing database nodes for sharded clusters; regional replication can thus multiply search compute as well as transfer exposure. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/cluster-config/multi-cloud-distribution.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/search-node.md

Same-region placement does not guarantee free networking: AWS charges applicable peering transfers while exempting same-AZ peering, and Google Cloud distinguishes free qualifying same-zone VM traffic from charged cross-zone traffic. Provider tariffs explain topology effects but are not substitutes for Atlas invoice rates. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30) Sources: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonVPC/latest/PeeringGuide/Welcome.html ; https://cloud.google.com/vpc/pricing

Google Cloud's VM tariff lists $0.01/GiB for different zones in one region, $0.02/GiB between North American regions, and $0.05/GiB between North America and Europe. These are cloud-VM comparison inputs, not quoted Atlas Search Node prices. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

AWS charges nothing to create a VPC peering connection, but data transfer across peering connections is charged (same-AZ peering transfer is free). A beSharp blog example for an Atlas M10 compares a public endpoint routed through a NAT Gateway with VPC peering. It says peering avoids NAT Gateway costs and leaves only AWS cross-AZ transfer charges of $0.01/GB in each direction, and it models these as blog-level list-price estimates. Actual savings depend on the real traffic route and existing infrastructure. Sources: https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/faqs/ ; https://blog.besharp.it/aws-data-transfer-costs-from-a-nutshell-to-the-calculator-through-3-real-world-scenarios/

MongoDB recommends same-provider, same-region application placement, smaller projected result payloads, and client-driver compression to reduce transferred bytes. Its cost guidance states that intra-cluster communication is already compressed; client compression should not be credited again as a new internal Search Node saving. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

A 2020 Atlas forum complaint attributed network-out charges to search indexing, while a MongoDB reply described search reading only the local mongod. The thread establishes a historical attribution dispute, not a demonstrated billing defect or a current exemption for dedicated Search Nodes. (medium confidence)

For TCO, estimate Search Node network cost as the volume of data transferred between Search Nodes and database nodes times the applicable per-GB rate, which Atlas sets by cloud provider and by the region of the source and destination nodes, and add Search Node hours (number of nodes and search tier) separately. This is a modeling inference; the sources do not establish a universal consolidation savings percentage. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/search-node.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs.md

Consolidating search into Atlas does not establish a zero-transfer-cost architecture: dedicated Search Nodes have billable internal traffic, and Atlas transfer pricing depends on the cloud provider and source/destination regions. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/search-node.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs.md

Atlas requires at least two Search Nodes per region and charges hourly for each Search Node. For sharded multi-region clusters, it deploys the configured Search Node count in each region containing database nodes; regional expansion therefore adds a capacity cost as well as possible transfer costs. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/cluster-config/multi-cloud-distribution.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/search-node.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs.md

MongoDB announced multi-region availability for Search Nodes on all three major cloud providers (AWS, Google Cloud and Azure). Availability by region is still limited: Atlas documentation says dedicated Search Nodes are available in all supported Google Cloud regions but only a subset of AWS and Azure regions, so the announcement does not mean every cloud region supports them. Multi-cloud cluster configuration lets you deploy electable, read-only, analytics and Search Nodes as workload purposes. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/product-release-announcements/atlas-search-nodes-now-with-multi-region-availability ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-vector-search/deployment-options.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/cluster-config/multi-cloud-distribution.md

Same-region placement does not universally make network traffic free. AWS charges VPC peering traffic crossing availability zones, while Google prices eligible same-region inter-zone VM traffic at $0.01 per GiB. These cloud-provider rules describe connectivity costs, not a substitute tariff for the Atlas invoice. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30) Sources: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/demystifying-amazon-vpc-peering-charges/ ; https://cloud.google.com/vpc/network-pricing

AWS says creating a VPC peering connection is free, and peered traffic remaining within one availability zone is free even across accounts; crossing availability zones or AWS regions incurs transfer charges. Private peering alone is therefore insufficient evidence of zero network cost. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-03-19)

Google lists no charge for eligible same-zone VM traffic using internal IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. Its separate inter-region VM transfer table varies by source and destination geography, and external-address paths can use internet rates. Cost estimates must retain the actual route and GiB billing unit. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)
